summary:
Allie Howe, VCISO at Growth Cyber, presents a framework for building trustworthy AI, defined as the combination of AI security (how the outside world harms AI applications) and AI safety (how AI applications harm the world). She motivates the topic with real-world incidents: a chatbot offering a Chevy Tahoe for one dollar, Slack leaking private channel data via prompt injection, and Epic Labs' AI Darth Vader in Fortnite exhibiting offensive behavior. A 2024 lawsuit against OpenAI was dismissed, establishing that deploying organizations are responsible for AI outputs both legally and reputationally.

The three-pillar framework spans the AI lifecycle. MLSecOps (build phase) covers model provenance, exposed secrets, and model serialization attacks — where malicious code embedded in serialized models executes on deserialization. Howe demonstrates Protect AI's ModelScan tool for detecting unsafe operators. AI Red Teaming (test phase) simulates adversarial threats and safety concerns, informs runtime guardrails, and helps compare LLMs. AI Runtime Security (run phase) is identified as the highest-priority investment, being easy to implement via API integration while providing strong shift-right protection against prompt injections, jailbreaks, and unsafe prompts.

Howe walks through the estimated Fortnite Darth Vader architecture: user audio flows through Fortnite servers to ElevenLabs for voice-to-text, then to Gemini for response generation, and back through the same path. Runtime security can be inserted at multiple points, balancing cost, latency, and accuracy. She demonstrates Pillar Security's runtime solution with an ALS clinical trials agent, showing custom guardrails blocking unauthorized database modifications and restricting topics like competitor mentions.

Beyond technical controls, Howe emphasizes GRC integration: validating AI outputs can be logged as custom controls in platforms like Vanta, supporting SOC 2 compliance and showcased in trust centers as a competitive sales advantage. She argues cybersecurity and business risk are now aligned — off-topic AI outputs don't generate revenue. The regulatory landscape is expanding with ISO 42001, the EU AI Act, HIPAA, and FDA AI/ML guidelines. In closing, Howe reiterates that trustworthy AI is essential to create things never thought possible, urges organizations not to wait for a lawsuit, and recaps the three-pillar approach as the path forward.

sections.title: Introduction & Trustworthy AI in the News
sections.summary: Allie Howe introduces herself as VCISO at Growth Cyber. She motivates trustworthy AI with real-world incidents: a Chevy Tahoe chatbot sold for one dollar, Slack leaking private data via prompt injection, and Epic Labs' AI Darth Vader in Fortnite exhibiting offensive behavior. A lawsuit against OpenAI was dismissed, establishing user responsibility for AI outputs.

sections.title: Responsibility & Team Roles in Trustworthy AI
sections.summary: Howe argues that deploying organizations are responsible for AI outputs legally and reputationally. Trustworthy AI requires collaboration across product (relevance, helpfulness), security (prompt injections, jailbreaks), and engineering (cost, latency) teams. She defines the core recipe: AI security plus AI safety.

sections.title: From DevSecOps to MLSecOps: Three-Pillar Framework
sections.summary: AI engineering introduces a new paradigm since AI engineers work in Databricks and Jupyter notebooks rather than traditional CI/CD. Howe presents three pillars: MLSecOps (build), AI Red Teaming (test), and AI Runtime Security (run). Unlike shift-left traditional security, AI's non-determinism demands strong runtime protections.

sections.title: MLSecOps & Model Serialization Attacks
sections.summary: MLSecOps covers model provenance, exposed secrets in AI environments, and model serialization attacks. Serialization attacks embed malicious code in models (e.g., pickle format) that executes on deserialization, causing data loss, credential leaks, or model poisoning. Howe demonstrates Protect AI's ModelScan tool detecting unsafe operators, noting its Hugging Face integration.

sections.title: AI Red Teaming & Runtime Security Priority
sections.summary: AI Red Teaming tests adversarial threats (prompt injections, jailbreaks) and safety concerns (harmful content, bias). Benefits include informing runtime guardrails, comparing LLMs to detect backdoors, and continuous testing as models evolve. Howe identifies runtime security as the highest-priority investment area, noting red teaming's cost and complexity.

sections.title: AI Runtime Security Implementation & Fortnite Architecture
sections.summary: Runtime security is easy to implement via API or Python module. It defends against indirect prompt injections (via RAG/web data), direct prompt injections, jailbreaks (shown with Lera AI example), and unsafe/off-topic prompts. Howe walks through the estimated Fortnite Darth Vader architecture: user audio flows through Fortnite servers to ElevenLabs (voice-to-text), then Gemini (response generation), and back. Runtime security can be inserted at multiple points, validating both AI safety and AI security.

sections.title: Runtime Security Trade-offs & Pillar Security Demo
sections.summary: Runtime security solutions balance cost, latency, and accuracy, and are backed by research teams tracking new jailbreaks and prompt injections. Howe demonstrates Pillar Security with an ALS clinical trials agent that should only recommend patients for studies — not modify data. Pillar blocks an attempt to change a patient's FC percentage in the database. Custom guardrails can detect PII, restrict topics, prevent database modifications, and enforce business goals.

sections.title: GRC Integration, Trust Centers & Competitive Advantage
sections.summary: Howe shows how trustworthy AI controls integrate with GRC platforms like Vanta. A custom SOC 2 control for validating AI outputs can be evidenced and displayed in a trust center, demonstrating AI security to prospects, reducing security questionnaires, and creating competitive advantage in sales cycles.

sections.title: Why Trustworthy AI Matters: Regulation & Innovation
sections.summary: Howe argues cybersecurity and business risk are now aligned — AI outputs that are off-topic or unsafe don't generate revenue. AI magnifies missing cybersecurity best practices like supply chain and data tracking. The regulatory landscape is expanding with ISO 42001, the EU AI Act (20M fine for a face-scraping company), HIPAA, and FDA AI/ML guidelines. Trustworthy AI is essential to unlock revolutionary healthcare innovation, including models trained on 1.3 million cells for organ transplantation breakthroughs.

sections.title: Conclusion: Call to Action & Recap
sections.summary: Howe closes by stating that trust must be in place from the beginning to enable revolutionary innovation. She reiterates that deploying organizations are responsible for building trustworthy AI, citing dismissed lawsuits where users bore responsibility. She urges the audience not to wait for a lawsuit and recaps the framework: trustworthy AI equals AI security plus AI safety, achievable through MLSecOps, AI red teaming, and AI runtime security at deployment. She shares her contact handles and invites further questions.
